newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans unsure of new French govt's Europolicies.
newsitem.headline: Germans unsure of new French govt's Europolicies.

text.p: German media and analysts looked sceptically on Thursday at the communists in France's new Socialist-led government but were unsure if their influence would make Bonn's closest partner less pro-European.

"Communists in French government" was the front-page headline in many newspapers in Germany, where 40 years of East-West division made most voters highly sensitive to the idea of giving Marxists any power at all.

Views were divided on whether the communists' stand against the Maastricht Treaty on closer European union meant Prime Minister Lionel Jospin would want to weaken the planned euro currency beyond the tight limits that Germany has tried to impose for it.

Deutschlandfunk radio expressed disappointment that former European Commission president Jacques Delors was not named foreign minister, saying "he would have been the guarantee for a consistent continuation of France's european policy."
It said the new foreign minister, Hubert Vedrine, ranks as a convinced pro-European but judged his European affairs minister Pierre Moscovici to be less so.

Bonn's General-Anzeiger newspaper said: "There are no signs that Jospin wants to make radical changes in foreign and defence policy. His main goal is fighting unemployment. If European commitments from the Maastricht treaty upset this, the new government will try to weaken them or add additional elements."
The Saechsische Zeitung in Dresden in the ex-communist east said the cabinet showed Jospin wanted to maintain unity among leftists for and against further European integration.

"But the state's coffers are empty and (President Jacques) Chirac will put massive pressure on him to meet the euro criteria somehow. If Jospin has to tighten belts, that could be the end of this unity."

Joachim Schild, French affairs expert at the German-French Institute in Ludwigsburg, saw no fundamental change in France's pro-European policies but expected pressure for a wider interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.
"When one sees the composition of the government, one cannot say we can expect an anti-euro course," he said.

"Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine seems to me to give a guarantee that a pro-euro course will be continued," he told German Radio. "The lady who was in a leading position (during the Maastricht negotiations), Elisabeth Guigou, is in the cabinet, albeit not in foreign affairs.
"But that does not mean France will support the strict interpretation of Maastricht criteria, which the German government and the Bundesbank have tried to impose.

"They will stick to the goal of stability, but that doesn't necesssarily mean that the criterium of 3.0 (public deficit to gross domestic product) will be interpreted so strictly," he said, adding that Paris would also push for an employment chapter in the new Maastricht treaty which Germany has so far firmly opposed.
As for the communists in the cabinet, Schild said: "Their influence will be limited."
